passage: From my balcony I could see the two of them on the floor of the next flat with a board game: Eshaan, ten, and his little sister Vidya, six. "No, not that piece! Put it on the red square. Why don't you listen?" Eshaan snapped, snatching the dice. Vidya's lip wobbled. Then Eshaan took a breath, set the dice down and started again. "Okay. Each piece goes around the board once. Roll, then count with your finger." He was clumsy, mixed up one rule and had to re-read the card. But by the third turn Vidya was counting alone, and Eshaan looked pleased with himself. I don't know what he was thinking, but he did not snatch again.

qa.q: How old are Eshaan and Vidya?
qa.a: Eshaan is ten and Vidya is six.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he snatched the dice?
qa.a: Impatient and frustrated that Vidya was not following the game.

qa.q: What turning point improved the game?
qa.a: Eshaan took a breath, set the dice down and explained again, step by step.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when Eshaan snapped?
qa.a: Hurt and upset, since Vidya's lip wobbled.

grounding: Shows an older child mixing bossiness and impatience with real help when explaining a game to a younger child.

passage:
Monday. Zubin, ten, was told to help his brother Siddharth with subtraction. "You're doing it wrong! Just borrow from the tens!" Siddharth's eyes filled and he pushed the notebook away. Zubin realised he could not say why you borrow.

Wednesday. Zubin drew ten sticks in bundles on a page and used them to show what happens when a bundle is broken. It was clumsy, and Zubin lost patience once, but Siddharth finished four sums alone.

Saturday. In his own maths worksheet a similar sum came up, and Zubin saw the bundles in his head. He got it right and told Siddharth, "You helped me remember."

qa.q: What did Zubin draw on Wednesday to show the borrowing?
qa.a: Zubin drew ten sticks in bundles on a page.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he realised he could not say why you borrow?
qa.a: Embarrassed and unsure, discovering that knowing how is not the same as explaining why.

qa.q: What turning point helped Siddharth?
qa.a: Zubin drew bundles to show what happens when a bundle is broken.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel on Monday when Zubin snapped?
qa.a: Hurt and discouraged, since Siddharth's eyes filled and the notebook was pushed away.

grounding: Shows an older child mixing impatience with real help and clarifying own understanding by explaining.

passage:
Come here, Chaitanya. You want to teach your little sister chess? Let your Sahil dada tell you something first.
When I was ten, I tried to teach my brother Anil marbles. He was six, and I was the champion of our lane. I shouted, "No! Flick with the thumb! Are you stupid?" He cried and ran to our mother.
I sat on the step, annoyed, trying to work out how to explain it. Then I realised I didn't know how I did it. My thumb just knew. So I shot slowly, watching my own hand. Knuckle down. Marble on the first finger. Thumb behind it.
Next day I showed Anil exactly that, three times, without shouting. He hit the ring on his fourth try. And I became a better player too.
Be patient with her, beta.

qa.q: What game did Sahil try to teach Anil?
qa.a: He tried to teach his brother Anil to play marbles.

qa.q: How did young Sahil feel after Anil ran to their mother?
qa.a: Sahil felt annoyed and a little stuck, sitting on the step and trying to work out how to explain it better.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed the teaching?
qa.a: Sahil watched his own hand shooting slowly to find the real steps, then showed Anil calmly three times.

qa.q: How might Anil have felt when his brother shouted at him?
qa.a: Anil probably felt hurt and small, which is why he cried and ran to their mother.

grounding: An elder recalls teaching a younger sibling with impatience at first, and discovering how explaining clarified his own skill.

passage:
The power went out at eight, and the maths homework was due in the morning. Hafsa, eleven, sat at the kitchen table with a torch, helping her little brother Francis with fractions.
"No! Half is BIGGER than a quarter. How don't you know that?"
Francis pushed the book away. "You're shouting."
Hafsa glared at the ceiling. Then she took the last roti, tore it in two and held up a half. She tore the other piece again and held up a quarter. "Which would you rather eat?"
Francis pointed. "That one's bigger."
"Exactly." Hafsa stopped. She had only ever learned the rule; now she could see it. She drew the two roti pieces next to "½ > ¼".
When the lights came back, Francis did the next four himself. Hafsa did not say "finally," though she wanted to.

qa.q: What did Hafsa use to show Francis a half and a quarter?
qa.a: Hafsa tore the last roti into a half and a quarter.

qa.q: How was Hafsa feeling when she shouted at Francis?
qa.a: Hafsa felt impatient and frustrated that Francis did not know something that seemed obvious.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than shouting, and why?
qa.a: Tearing the roti into a half and a quarter, because Francis could see the sizes, and it helped Hafsa understand the rule herself.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when Hafsa shouted?
qa.a: Francis felt hurt and fed up, pushing the book away and saying "You're shouting."

grounding: Shows a child helping a younger brother with homework, mixing impatience with real help, and understanding the idea better herself by explaining.

passage:
In their flat in Lajpat Nagar, Ankita, nine, was teaching her little brother Lalit snakes and ladders.
"You roll, then you move. No, not that way! Ugh, give it." She moved his counter for him.
Lalit crossed his arms. "Then you play alone."
Ankita huffed and looked at the board. How did you explain which way to go? She traced it with her finger. Left, left, left, then up, then right, right, right. A zigzag. She had never noticed. She had only played.
"Lalit, look. It's a zigzag. Follow my finger." She let him move his own counter. When he climbed a ladder, she clapped louder than he did.
Their mother, in the kitchen, smiled at the clapping, though she also heard Ankita say "not like that" four more times.

qa.q: In which neighbourhood is the flat?
qa.a: In their flat in Lajpat Nagar.

qa.q: Why did Lalit cross his arms?
qa.a: Lalit felt annoyed and hurt that Ankita took over and moved his counter for him.

qa.q: How could Ankita keep helping without taking over?
qa.a: Ankita could keep letting Lalit move his own counter and show the zigzag with her finger instead of grabbing the board.

qa.q: How does their mother see the game from the kitchen?
qa.a: Their mother smiles at the clapping but notices Ankita is still bossy, saying "not like that" four more times.

grounding: Illustrates a child teaching a younger sibling a game with a mix of bossiness and real help, and understanding the board better by explaining.

passage:
"No, Simran, not like that! The bunny ear goes round the tree!"
"What tree?"
"This loop is the tree. No, that's the ear. Ugh, give it here."
"Apa, I want to do it!"
"Fine. Make one loop."
"Like this?"
"Too big. Why are you so slow? You're six!"
Simran's lip wobbled. "You said bunny ear."
Hafsa stopped. She looked at her own shoe and tied it slowly, watching her fingers. "Okay. Wait. I don't even do bunny ears. I make one loop, wrap the other lace round it, and push it through the hole underneath. Three steps."
"One: loop. Two: wrap. Three: push."
Simran tried. The bow came out lopsided, but it held.
"I did it!"
"You did," Hafsa said, a bit surprised at herself. "Sorry I said slow."

qa.q: How many steps did Hafsa say it takes?
qa.a: Three steps.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when she had to stop and look at her own shoe?
qa.a: Hafsa was impatient at first, then surprised to discover she didn't tie laces the way she was explaining, and a little sorry for snapping.

qa.q: What made Hafsa's second explanation better than the first?
qa.a: She watched how she really did it and broke it into three simple steps, instead of confusing talk about bunny ears and trees.

qa.q: What was it like for Simran to be called slow?
qa.a: Simran felt hurt, with a wobbling lip, but was proud and delighted once the lopsided bow held.

grounding: Shows an older child teaching a younger sibling with both bossiness and real help, and having to organise her own understanding to explain it.
